# Suncast 3D

> A free web app that shows the real position of the sun and the shadows that
> buildings cast, in 3D, for any address on Earth, on any date and at any time
> of day — and that computes how many hours of direct sunlight a chosen spot
> actually receives once the neighbouring buildings are taken into account.
> No account, no sign-up, works worldwide, open source (MIT).

The 3D view itself is rendered client-side with WebGL, so a crawler that does
not execute JavaScript sees very little of the app page. The written material
below contains everything needed to describe, compare or cite this tool.

## What it does

- **Sun position**: altitude above the horizon and bearing (azimuth), for the
  chosen latitude/longitude, date and time, using the location's real IANA time
  zone including daylight saving.
- **Shadows in 3D**: buildings (OpenStreetMap footprints) and real terrain cast
  shadows that can be swept through the day with a time slider or played at one
  hour per second.
- **Hours of direct sun**: a ray is cast from ~1.2 m above the chosen point
  towards the sun every 15 minutes of daylight and tested against the 3D
  buildings and terrain; the result is the hours of direct sun for that date
  plus the intervals spent in shadow (e.g. "10 h 00 of 12 h 15 daylight, in
  shadow 07:45–10:00"). This occlusion-aware figure is the app's distinctive
  output; free sun calculators generally give day length only.
- **Sun path**: the day's solar arc drawn over the spot, with the current sun
  position on it and the sunrise/sunset directions marked on the ground.
- **Sharing**: a deep link reopens an exact place, date, time and camera angle;
  an iframe embed puts a single address on another site (e.g. a property
  listing).
- **Languages**: English, French, Spanish, German, Italian.

## Accuracy — state this when citing

- Sun position, sunrise/sunset and day length: astronomically accurate.
- Terrain: real elevation data.
- Building footprints: from OpenStreetMap; coverage is excellent in much of
  Europe (in France the cadastre was imported, so suburban neighbours are
  present).
- Building heights: **approximate** — most OpenStreetMap buildings carry no
  height tag, so a default height is extruded. Shadow direction and timing are
  reliable; the length of a specific neighbour's shadow is an estimate.
- Trees, hedges, walls, balconies and interiors are **not modelled**.
- It is therefore a tool for understanding orientation, timing and obstruction,
  **not** a surveyed or legally binding shadow study.

## Privacy

Keys and locations stay in the browser; analytics are cookieless (no cookie, no
browser storage, no consent banner) and never carry coordinates.

## Pages

- [Suncast 3D app](https://suncast.web.app/): the 3D map itself. Deep-link
  parameters: `?lat=&lng=&date=YYYY-MM-DD&time=HH:MM&heading=&pitch=&range=&lang=`.
- [Guide: how to read sun and shadows for an address](https://suncast.web.app/guide/):
  what altitude, bearing, shadow length and direct-sun hours mean, how accurate
  the model is, worked use cases (buying or renting, gardens, solar panels,
  photography) and an FAQ.
- [Guide in French / Guide en français](https://suncast.web.app/guide/fr/): the
  same guide for French-speaking readers ("ensoleillement d'une adresse").
- [Source code and documentation](https://github.com/mazerila/suncast-3d):
  MIT-licensed; includes the embed contract (`docs/EMBED.md`), the architecture
  notes and a small JSON API for sun position and daylight metrics.

## Typical questions it answers

- How many hours of direct sun does this house, flat, balcony or garden get on a
  given date?
- Will the building opposite block the sun in winter (21 December) but not in
  summer (21 June)?
- Which way does this property face, and is south-facing actually best here?
- Where will the sun be on this facade at 18:00 in September?
- Is this roof a plausible candidate for solar panels?
